item.title: [Call for Papers] 10th International ASTRIL Conference (Rome, January 2027)
item.description:
21-22 January, 2027 | Rome, Italy

Conference theme: Protecting Workers in Times of Conflict: Minimum Wages, Wage Indexation and Collective Bargaining

European countries and the world at large are facing a period of renewed economic, social and geopolitical instability. Armed conflicts, energy shocks, disruptions to global trade, and related inflationary pressures have placed increasing strain on employment prospects, wages and living standards. At the same time, following the post-pandemic recovery, Italy and Europe are again experiencing slower economic growth. These processes are occurring against the background of an erosion of the industrial base and the relocation of production that have been under way for several years in some of the main advanced economies, producing profound changes in the organisation of labour markets and the distribution of employment. Moreover, they are occurring at a time when workers and trade unions in these economies have already experienced a weakening of their bargaining power over recent decades, reshaping income distribution between and within countries, at both the personal and functional levels.

These developments call for a broader debate on how wage-setting institutions can protect workers and on which policies can support employment, productive transformation and macroeconomic stability. They also point to a socio-institutional and legal reconfiguration of labour relations — one that concerns not only the economics of wage-setting but also the dignity of work and the effectiveness of the rights that protect it. Minimum wages, wage indexation and collective bargaining offer different, and potentially complementary, forms of protection. Their effects have long been debated along two axes: on the one hand, employment, hours, hiring and turnover; on the other, the distribution of income — across the wage distribution and between labour and capital — together with household income, prices, profits, productivity, job quality and the allocation of workers across firms and sectors. These two dimensions are not separate: how these institutions shape employment and how they shape distribution are increasingly understood as aspects of a single question. Their effectiveness depends, in turn, on enforcement, bargaining coverage, the structure of product and labour markets, and the broader fiscal and monetary policy framework.

The present period of conflict is therefore understood in a broad sense, spanning geopolitical conflicts and their economic consequences, distributive conflict between wages and profits, and the institutional tensions surrounding the determination of fair and adequate pay. The conference aims to examine how these conflicts affect workers and how labour institutions and public policies can contribute to more equitable and sustainable outcomes.

The organizers cordially invite scholars from economics, law, and the social sciences — including labour law, industrial relations, sociology, political science and economic history — to submit theoretical, empirical and policy-oriented contributions.

Topics

  1. Minimum Wages, Employment and Income Distribution
  2. Wage Indexation, Inflation and Macroeconomic Adjustment
  3. Collective Bargaining, Industrial Relations and Worker Power
  4. Legal and Institutional Frameworks for Fair and Adequate Wages

Please write the topic that the paper refers to (1, 2, 3, 4) in the abstract and send it, or session proposals (4 papers at least), to: astril@uniroma3.it. If the abstract refers generically to the evolving labour market, state that it concerns topic 5.

item.description:
Deadline: 4 February 2027

17-18 June, 2027 | Vienna, Austria

This two-day conference of the Society for the History of Recent Social Science (HISRESS), at the University of Vienna in Austria, will bring together researchers working on the history of post-World War II social science. It will provide a forum for the latest research on the cross-disciplinary history of the post-war social sciences, including but not limited to anthropology, economics, psychology, political science, and sociology as well as related fields like area studies, communication studies, design, history, international relations, law, linguistics, and urban studies. The conference, aims to build upon the recent emergence of work and conversation on cross-disciplinary themes in the postwar history of the social sciences.

Submissions are welcome in such areas including, but not restricted to:

  • Social scientific knowledge for intervention within various political regimes and political economies
  • The interchange of social science concepts and figures between the academy and wider intellectual and popular spheres
  • Comparative institutional histories of departments and programs
  • Border disputes and boundary work between disciplines as well as academic cultures
  • Themes and concepts developed in the history and sociology of the natural sciences, reconceptualized for the social science context
  • Professional and applied training programs and schools, and the quasi-disciplinary fields (like business administration) that typically housed them
  • The traffic of social science into science and technology programs
  • The role of social science in post-colonial state-building and governance
  • The role of disciplinary memory
  • Engagements with matters of gender, sexuality, race, religion, nationality, disability and other markers of identity and difference
  • Social sciences, activism, counter-expertise, and counter-knowledge
  • Law and the social sciences

The two-day conference will be organized as a series of one-hour, single-paper sessions attended by all participants. Ample time will be set aside for intellectual exchange between presenters and attendees, as all participants are expected to prepare unpublished papers (not longer than 10,000 words, excluding footnotes and references) for circulation to other participants and read all pre-circulated papers in advance.

Proposals should contain no more than 1000 words, indicating the originality of the paper. The deadline for receipt of abstracts is February 4, 2027. Final notification will be given in March 2027 after proposals have been reviewed. Completed papers will be expected by June 4, 2027.

item.title: [Call for Papers] 16th International Conference on Political Economy: "Geopolitical Shifts, Green Transitions, and the New Global Order" (Online, Feburary 2027)
item.description:
Deadline: 17 February 2027

23 - 24 Feburary, 2027 | Online

The International Conference on Political Economy (ICOPEC) is delighted to announce its 2027 edition, themed “Geopolitical Shifts, Green Transitions, and the New Global Order.” This year’s conference seeks to delve into the most pressing challenges and transformations shaping our world today, exploring the multifaceted intersections of global power realignments, ecological imperatives, and the evolving global economic landscape.

The contemporary world is witnessing seismic shifts in the political and economic order. Rising geopolitical tensions, the decline of unipolarity, and the resurgence of regional alliances are reshaping the frameworks of international governance and cooperation. Simultaneously, the urgent need for sustainable development in the face of climate crises is driving an unprecedented green transition, which is redefining industries, labour markets, and trade systems. These transformations are further complicated by the rapid advancement of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, which are both empowering and disrupting societies globally.

Against this backdrop, persistent inequalities in wealth, opportunity, and environmental burdens highlight the necessity of addressing questions of social justice. Vulnerable populations, marginalised communities, and the Global South often bear the brunt of economic disruptions, environmental degradation, and migration crises, underscoring the need for inclusive solutions to these challenges. At the same time, grassroots movements, innovative policies, and interdisciplinary research offer hope for equitable and sustainable transitions.

ICOPEC invites scholars, policymakers, and practitioners to critically engage with these intertwined dynamics and explore pathways to a resilient and inclusive global order. This year’s theme seeks to address key questions:

  • How are shifting geopolitical alliances shaping the global response to climate change and sustainability?
  • What are the political, economic, and ethical implications of the green transition across nations, regions, and industries?
  • How do global trends in technology, health, urbanisation, and trade interact with the pursuit of equity and sustainability?

By integrating perspectives from economics, sociology, political science, environmental studies, law, philosophy, and other disciplines, this conference aims to foster a vibrant dialogue on the challenges and opportunities of this critical moment in history. Papers addressing theoretical, empirical, and interdisciplinary approaches are encouraged, as are those offering innovative methodologies or proposing actionable solutions to these global issues.

item.description:
Deadline: 30 December 2026

16-18 June, 2027 | Torino, Italy

Conference theme: Navigating Systemic Chaos: Hegemony, Crises and the Transformation of the World System

The First International Giovanni Arrighi Conference, to be held in Turin on 16, 17 and 18 June 2027, invites scholars from different disciplines, theoretical traditions and geographical contexts to examine the contemporary conjuncture and historical precedents through the concept of systemic chaos and, more broadly, through a critical engagement with Giovanni Arrighi’s intellectual legacy.

Rather than treating Arrighi’s work as a closed theoretical system or an object of commemoration, the conference seeks to place it in dialogue, tension and confrontation with contemporary problems and alternative traditions of thought. Arrighi’s own work crossed the conventional boundaries separating sociology, history, political economy, geography, anthropology and international relations. In the same spirit, the conference particularly welcomes interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary approaches capable of connecting transformations occurring at different geographical scales and across different spheres of social life.

Possible themes include, but are not limited to:

  • Hegemonic transitions and the changing world order
  • The material foundations of world order
  • Uneven development and changing regional orders
  • Financialisation and systemic chaos
  • Imperialism and militarisation
  • Class, labour and social conflict in the twenty-first century
  • Ideologies and political forms in periods of systemic crisis
  • Systemic chaos and socio-ecological crisis
  • Gender, race and intersectional perspectives on systemic transformation

These themes are intended as invitations rather than boundaries. The organizers particularly encourage contributions that connect several of these dimensions, explore neglected regions and historical experiences, compare the contemporary transition with previous episodes of systemic chaos, or critically revise the conceptual tools through which global transformations are conventionally understood.

The organizers welcome proposals for:

  • Individual papers: abstract of approximately 300–500 words, together with a short biographical note;

item.title: [Call for Papers] 2nd SLOW Symposium: "Researching SLOW by the Sea: Methods, Practices, and Philosophies for Socioecological Research in Organization" (Wales, May 2027)
item.description:
18-19 May 2027 | Swansea, Wales

Organisation scholars are increasingly confronting social and ecological crises as interconnected challenges that surround, shape, and increasingly penetrate organisational life (Campbell et al., 2019; Ergene et al., 2020; George et al., 2016). Contemporary scholarship and organisational practice is seeking to understand how organisations can mitigate, social and planetary ill-health (Ergene et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2024; Dentoni et al., 2026) and pursue forms of organisation, leadership and work oriented towards socioecological justice.

Yet, the practices and institutions on academic research sit uneasily alongside commitments to socioecological justice. The well-documented ‘publish or perish’ culture is just the most obvious sign of a neoliberal, ‘dark’ academia: a seemingly neutral, metrics-obsessed, zombified bureaucracy that threatens academic freedom (Charitsis & Bradshaw, 2026; Fleming, 2021) where an extractive and instrumental view of theoretical and ‘real-world’ impact dominates (Brauer et al., 2026; Ioannidis, 2012). Such conditions increasingly shape the research process: both what research is conducted, and how. With limited funding for slow, exploratory, and conceptual research, scholars ‘helicopter’ into and out of the field. It becomes seductive to conduct hasty analysis, fitting empirical findings into pre-established frameworks or process models. Theoretical or empirical insights are rushed to market without sufficient fermentation time, yielding bland results. Reciprocity – what researchers owe the communities they work with – chokes beneath layers of bureaucracy, temporal and financial impossibilities, and peculiar interpretations of how individual institutions dogmatise their call for academic staff’s contributions to evaluations of research – in the UK, the all-powerful Research Excellence Framework. All the while, concerns for social and ecological justice are increasingly shaping organisational practice. It becomes perilous to navigate this changing landscape and pursue sociecological research and practice.

Therefore, the 2nd SLOW Symposium asks: If socioecological justice calls for new ways of organising, leading, and working, how do they also demand new ways of researching? What would it mean to undertake research that is itself attentive to socioecological justice? What methodological, practical, and philosophical commitments might characterize genuinely SLOW research? What enduring ‘real-world(s)’ should SLOW research and praactice build that resist capitalist and (neoliberal) State capture?

Taking up these questions, we invite contributions to the symposium that engage with the possibilities, challenges, and implications of SLOW research and practice. These may include, but are certainly not limited to, several overarching themes:

Philosophies

  • Philosophical foundations for socioecological research
  • Ethics, ontology, and epistemology in the context of ecological and social crises in organisation
  • Posthuman, relational, Indigenous, feminist, and other critical perspectives
  • Rethinking the purposes and responsibilities of academic knowledge production

Methods

  • Translating principles of socioecological justice into research design and methodology
  • Pedagogical methods that stimulate learning for socioecological transformation
  • Non-representational and other anti-capitalist methodologies
  • Participatory, collaborative, and community-engaged approaches
  • Methodological experimentation and innovation in socioecological research
  • Reflexive and embodied research practices

Practices

  • Case studies and practitioner perspectives on organising for socioecological justice
  • Transforming research processes through engagement with participants, communities, and ecologies
  • Navigating temporal pressures and institutional constraints
  • Building relationships of care, reciprocity, and responsibility in research
  • Challenges and opportunities in conducting slower forms of inquiry

Submission information

All attendees are asked to make a contribution to the symposium. Using this registration form, you will be asked to:

  • Provide your contact details
  • Indicate the nature of your contribution (e.g. academic paper, provocation, practitioner perspective, creative piece). We will shape the programme to reflect the range of submissions received.
  • Submit a 500-word abstract by 31 January, 2027 using the registration form. Abstracts may present academic work or practictioner perspectives related to the symposium theme. Indicate whether you have institutional support to pay the £150 registration fee (we will email you about payment), or if you are seeking a fee waiver. If you are requesting a fee waiver, please provide a short (e.g. 1 sentence) explanation. We aim to grant fee waivers to all attendees that need them.

item.title: [Call for Papers] 39th EAEPE Annual Conference (Poznań, September 2027)
item.description:
Deadline: 15 December 2026

15-17 September, 2027 | Poznań, Poland

Conference theme: Between Security and Solidarity: The Social Contract Under Geopolitical and Technological Pressures

Geoeconomic competition now shapes which technologies are built, by whom, and for what. Sanctions, export controls, investment screening, and technology restrictions have become primary instruments of interstate rivalry, concentrated on semiconductors, artificial intelligence, battery and grid technologies, and clean energy infrastructure. At stake is not market share but control over the productive capabilities on which future economies rest.

Societies need the same technologies for different purposes. Heatwaves, wildfires, drought, and flooding have made climate change a lived condition that demands rapid deployment of clean energy and adaptation infrastructure. Automation and AI threaten to displace work faster than labour market institutions and social protection can absorb. These claims collide. Export controls slow the diffusion of green technology to countries that need it most; subsidies follow strategic advantage rather than social need; defence spending competes with climate adaptation and social protection for constrained budgets; and the industrial policy tools now embraced across the global North were long denied to developing economies. Whether transformation can be steered toward social and ecological ends is ultimately a question about the social contract: what can people still expect from economic institutions when security claims the first call on resources?

These pressures also test economics itself. Frameworks that treat technology as exogenous, geopolitics as external, and markets as self-correcting cannot explain a world in which productive capacity is a security asset. This conference invites contributions that rethink economics through evolutionary, institutional, and other heterodox approaches that place power and the co-evolution of institutions and technologies at the centre.

Topics

  • Geoeconomics, sanctions and economic coercion: effects on third countries, peripheries and vulnerable groups
  • Industrial policy and development space: securitisation of technology governance and catch-up development
  • Climate change, adaptation and the energy transition: green finance, climate risk and distributional effects
  • Technology, automation and the future of work: AI and job displacement, skills, job quality and social protection
  • Labour markets, inequality and bargaining power: segmentation, precarious and platform work, gendered divisions of labour
  • Finance and transformation: capital allocation, financialisation and financial stability under geopolitical uncertainty
  • Institutions, fiscal capacity and governance: welfare and care regimes, and competing claims of defence, adaptation and social spending
  • Global and comparative perspectives: South–North and East–West dynamics, uneven development and migration
  • Rethinking economic theory and method: power, agency and co-evolution; pluralism; the boundaries between economics, technology and security

item.title: [Call for Papers] Alternate Routes Conference 2027 (Barcelona, June 2027)
item.description:
Deadline: 31 December 2026

8-10 June, 2027 | Barcelona, Spain

Conference theme: The Cost of Living Under Capitalism - Crisis and Inequality in Everyday Life

The cost-of-living crisis is not simply a temporary inflationary shock but the product of longer-term transformations in housing, labour markets, welfare states, finance and systems of social reproduction. While rising living costs have intensified economic insecurity, its effects are unevenly distributed across class, race, gender, age, citizenship, disability and geography. Widening inequality has fuelled renewed debates about work, social policy, democracy and economic organization, while contributing to political polarization and the growth of populist and far-right movements. These developments are inseparable from a broader context of war, militarization and geopolitical rivalry, whose economic costs are often borne most heavily by working-class and marginalized populations.

This conference invites researchers and activists to examine the causes, consequences and contestations surrounding the contemporary cost-of-living crisis. Rather than treating current hardships as a temporary disruption, the organizers encourage contributors to situate them within broader processes of capitalist restructuring, including financialization, austerity, labour market transformation, privatization, commodity speculation and the concentration of wealth and corporate power. At the same time, the crisis has generated new forms of resistance, organizing and political mobilization, prompting critical reflection on alternative economic and social futures.

Alternate Routes invites submissions that deepen our understanding of the relationship between the cost-of-living crisis and entrenched inequalities, while exploring collective responses, policy alternatives and transformative visions of social and economic justice. The organizers are particularly interested in how these dynamics are experienced and contested in everyday life: in the arithmetic of rent, bills and groceries; in the pressures of debt, precarious work and unpaid care; and in the solidarities, struggles and alternatives that emerge in response to mounting insecurity. The organizers also ask how these conditions are being politicized: how progressive movements are translating demands for housing, food, energy and economic security into political action, and how the far right is seeking to channel the same grievances toward exclusionary, nationalist and authoritarian ends.

Topics of interest include, but are not limited to:

  • Housing rent and displacement
  • Work, wages and precarity
  • Inequality, exclusion and social stratification
  • Care work, social reproduction and families
  • Social policy, austerity and welfare states
  • Finance, inflation and capitalist restructuring
  • Climate, environmental and energy justice
  • Labour organizing, social movements and collective resistance
  • Democracy, governance and political contestation
  • War, colonialism and dispossession

item.title: [Call for Papers] Association for Institutional Thought (AFIT) 2027 Conference (Denver, March 2027)
item.description:
Deadline: 15 January 2027

31 March - 3 April, 2027 | Denver, US

Conference theme: Institutions in a New Gilded Age: Technology, Reproduction Crises, and Collective Action

This year’s theme examines how emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, intersect with intensifying capitalist extraction and exclusion across the political, economic, social, and ecological spheres. It explores the challenges of AI-driven displacement and reorganization of work, the crises of social reproduction, and the challenges of building sustained collective action in hyperpolitical times.

As capitalist encroachment on sites of social reproduction accelerates, wealth and power are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a minority. This concentration evokes a new Gilded Age in which the majority faces growing barriers to democratic participation in decisions shaping their social and economic livelihood. Amid the heightened concerns about the effects of mega-corporations deployment of AI on employment and livelihoods, these barriers raise urgent questions about who directs technological change, who benefits from it, and who bears its costs.

Mass political parties, labor unions, and grassroots organizations have historically provided institutional foundations for popular resistance. As many of these organizations have weakened, heightened politicization and resentment expressed in public discourse and episodic protests have often struggled to translate into sustained collective action. The theme asks how popular resistance can build durable institutions capable of challenging concentrated capitalist power and also expanding democratic participation.

The organizers encourage papers that tackle this theme’s questions. In addition, the organizers encourage papers that explore structural, class, gender, ecological, and societal dynamics and employ institutional, multi-disciplinary, and historical perspectives that broaden our understanding of these current systemic crises and overall economic and social provisioning.

Among the topics that the organizers encourage:

  • Impact of artificial intelligence on the economy/labor market and social provisioning
  • The political economy of evolving trade and global production restructuring

The Marx–Rubin International Colloquium will take place on March 17–18, 2027, at the University Campus of the Federal University of Mato Grosso do Sul (UFMS) in Campo Grande, MS, Brazil. The event will bring together Brazilian and international researchers for a broad debate on the contemporary relevance of Karl Marx and Isaak Rubin. The colloquium emerged directly from discussions initiated at the Fourth Meeting of ANPOF's Marxism Working Group, held in Campo Grande in October 2025. Among the debates at that meeting, the roundtables focusing on Marx's theory of value and the interpretation pioneered by Isaak Rubin stood out.

To continue these debates, the colloquium provides a space for dialogue and exchange among researchers from different institutions, enabling the presentation and discussion of research on Marx and Rubin, with an emphasis on value theory and its interpretations and developments. In addition to plenary sessions and lectures by invited Brazilian and international researchers, the colloquium will welcome paper submissions for oral presentations organized into four thematic areas. More than a venue for presenting research results, the First Marx–Rubin International Colloquium aims to foster dialogue, academic exchange and the collective construction of knowledge, renewing research and deepening discussions on the critique of political economy and its contemporary challenges.

The organizers invite researchers, faculty and graduate students to submit original contributions to the Marx–Rubin International Colloquium. All accepted papers will be presented orally and published in the official proceedings with ISBN and DOI registration.

The event will take place in Mexico City from April 26 to 30, 2027. It will be held from April 26 to 28 at the Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana (UAM), Azcapotzalco campus, and on April 29 and 30 at various partner locations, including other UAM campuses (Iztapalapa and Xochimilco) and the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) (FES Acatlán and the Institute for Economic Research).

The relationship between capitalism and fascism has returned to the forefront as authoritarian political projects gain ground across continents, with far-right actors increasingly open to aligning themselves with fascist traditions. Capitalist crises have long unfolded through the reshaping of capitalism's co-constitutive and contradictory elements, including class relations, accumulation, social reproduction, nature, and imperialism. While these contradictions coexist, intersect, and get displaced at the global level, we must also study how they are mediated, articulated, and transformed through contemporary reactionary authoritarian and fascist politics. The current conjuncture therefore raises broader questions about the trajectory of neoliberalism and the contemporary transformation of capitalism more broadly.

The conference focuses on how authoritarian and fascist projects traverses and mediates these different dimensions of capitalist crises by examining how they shape the relations between accumulation, class struggle, social reproduction, ecology, imperialism, and dependency. How are authoritarian politics reshaping neoliberalism and the relations between capital and labour? How might fascism reshape social reproduction, mediate the ecological crisis, or transform the distribution of the costs of the crisis? How do authoritarian and fascist projects influence imperialism, dependency, hegemony, and transformations of the world order?

The organizers welcome theoretical, historical, comparative, and empirical contributions. These may address, among other topics:

item.title: [Call for Papers] Investigación Económica: Call for contributions on "Honoring the Legacy of Anwar Shaikh"
item.description:
Deadline: 1 May 2027

Anwar Shaikh (1945-2026) was an outstanding economist of his generation. He made substantial, wide-ranging contributions to economic theory and measurement across several areas of economics. Shaikh’s last book, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict and Crises (Oxford, 2016), is a testament to the breadth and depth of his interests and contributions, as well as the vitality of his vision. The traditions of economic analysis that Shaikh drew from and contributed to will continue to grow in relevance.

Investigación Económica invites papers that engage with Shaikh’s contributions and extend their themes and ideas. In light of Shaikh’s range of work, the editors welcome papers in a variety of areas: theories of value and distribution, competition, effective demand, economic cycles, growth, foreign trade, and balance of payments. The editors also welcome contributions to the estimation of labor values and prices of production, wage and profit rate differentials within and between industries and nations, classical/Marxian macroeconomic aggregates and their trends over time, net social wage, foreign trade patterns, and exchange rates.

An online archive of Shaikh’s papers (including unpublished notes, correspondence, etc.) is available at the Levy Economics Institute’s website, and the editors encourage scholars to submit papers that utilize the archival material. item.title: [Call for Papers] Journal of the History of Economic Thought: Special Issue on "The economic foundations of the eugenics-immigration entanglement in the late nineteenth century and beyond"
item.description:
Deadline: 1 December 2026

For the special issue, the Journal of the History of Economic Thought invites contributions for two additional papers that explore the economic foundations of the entanglement of eugenics and immigration policy at the turn of the 20th century. The anti-immigration policies and accompanying rhetoric that emerged during this period provide important historical context for contemporary restrictionist arguments in the United States, Canada, Great Britain, Europe, and Australia. In the United States, between the 1890s and the early 1920s, organizations such as the Immigration Restriction League mobilized public concern over mass migration from Southern and Eastern Europe, arguing that unchecked immigration threatened American institutions, labor markets, and national cohesion. These arguments, often framed through the emerging authority of the social sciences and the language of eugenics, helped legitimize increasingly restrictive policies culminating in the Immigration Act of 1924. A similar story can be told for Great Britian, whose Aliens Order 1920 restricted the entry of individuals unable to support themselves, the medically unfit, and the criminal. Consider also the Canadian acts limiting immigration during this period: the Chinese Immigration Act (1885), the Immigration Acts (1906 and 1910), and the Gentlemen’s Agreement (1908).

Historicizing the first wave of immigration restrictionism reveals how demographic change, economic anxiety, racial prejudice, and claims of expert authority converge to shape policy. The editors argue that revisiting this earlier episode is particularly relevant given the reemergence of significant nativist and anti-immigrant sentiment across much of the world. While important preliminary work has been done on the topic, there is significant scope for both deeper and more wide-ranging explorations. The relation between eugenics and immigration that evolved during the Progressive Era in the United States, for example, impacted the dynamics of the growth of the American population, the functioning of the domestic labor market and raised questions about the need for new social policies and institutions. The accompanying social and economic regulations continue to influence American capitalism while the legacy of eugenics remains reflected in contemporary discussions of immigration. That this is not a solely North American phenomenon suggests a more globalized approach can deepen our understanding of the dynamics and impact of this key period in history.

The editors seek between two papers to complement and extend the following topics. Note that all papers will be subject to standard JHET review procedures and processes. A workshop for preliminary drafts is scheduled for Thursday, May 13, 2027 at the Universite Grenoble Alpes. The editors anticipate final papers should be submitted by late summer 2027.

  • Eugenics from the Other Shore. Italian Economists on Population and the Economic Consequences of Emigration, Manuela Mosca and Claudia Sunna (University of Salento)
  • Beyond the Melting Pot: Madison Grant and the Eugenic Theory of Immigration Restriction, Giovanni Cerro (Fondazione Collegio San Carlo di Modena)

item.title: [Call for Papers] Review of Evolutionary Political Economy: Special Issue on "Demand and Growth Regimes: Structural and International Dimensions"

While the literature on Demand and Growth Regimes (DGRs) and Growth Models (GMs) has significantly improved our understanding of demand formation and comparative growth dynamics, important questions remain regarding the relationship between DGRs, the structure of production and the international positioning of economies in real and financial terms. The special issue therefore focuses on the political economy and international positioning of DGRs/GMs, including the links to structural change, industrial strategies, international complementarities, currency hierarchies and geoeconomic dynamics. It will discuss theoretical and empirical contributions potentially ranging from large samples to comparative and single case studies of Global North and South countries.

The special issue aims to advance the debate on DGRs and GMA by bringing together junior and senior scholars from post-Keynesian economics, the regulation school, structuralist and dependency approaches, comparative political economy, and international political economy. It also welcomes contributions that engage with or originate from perspectives that have so far been underrepresented in the DGR/GM debate. We encourage submissions from evolutionary economics, ecological political economy, Global South and decolonial political economy traditions, labour process theory, social reproduction approaches, and research on contemporary geoeconomic transformations. Bringing these perspectives into dialogue can contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of capitalist development.

Contributions could address issues like:

  • Growth models and the role of institutions – has the demand orientation moved too far? How can institutions effectively be integrated into DGRs/GMs?
  • What are similarities and differences between the growth models approach, post-Keynesian demand regime analysis, French Regulation Theory and the Social Structures of Accumulation approach? What can GMA and DGR learn from the earlier approaches?
  • How can DGRs/GM analysis be adapted for the analysis of emerging and developing economies?
  • The political economy of DGRs/GMs and their transformations: dominant social blocs, growth coalitions, and development alliances – what are appropriate analytical frameworks for analysing the political foundations of growth models?
  • How, if at all, are growth models gendered? How can insights from feminist economics and feminist political economy be mobilised for DGRs/GM?
  • Do GMA and DGR have a growth fetish or can they deliver insights into the political economy of decarbonisation? What are the tensions between demand-led growth and ecological sustainability?

item.title: [Call for Papers] Review of Political Economy: Special Issue on "AI and the future of the university"
item.description:
Rationale
Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping how universities produce, certify and transmit knowledge, and this special issue asks who gains, who loses, and what kind of institution emerges. Large language models now draft papers, review manuscripts, grade essays and tutor students. Universities and publishers are adopting them faster than they can study their effects.

Public debate tends to treat AI as a technical shock that institutions must simply absorb. We start from a different premise: the adoption of AI in higher education is shaped by existing pressures — marketisation, casualised academic employment, metric-driven research evaluation, the concentrated market power of commercial publishers and platform firms, and chronic public underfunding. AI may intensify these pressures, redirect them, or open space to contest them.

The special issue invites contributions that examine these changes critically and in their institutional, economic and political context. We welcome work on the university as a workplace, as a producer of knowledge, as a site of teaching and learning, and as a public institution whose purpose is now being renegotiated.

Themes
We invite papers on any of the five themes below. The questions under each are indicative, not exhaustive.

1. AI, academic labour and the future of the university

AI changes what academic work is, who does it, and how it is valued. It may automate parts of teaching, research support and administration while creating new tasks of supervision, verification and data work.

  • How is AI changing the labour process, workload and autonomy of academic and professional staff?
  • Does AI deepen the casualisation of academic employment, or the divide between a secure core and a precarious periphery?
  • How are managerial control, performance metrics and surveillance being reorganised around AI tools?
  • What forms of collective bargaining, union strategy or professional resistance areemerging?
  • Who captures the productivity gains from AI in universities: staff, students,administrators or technology vendors?

2. AI, the production of knowledge and the future of journals
AI is entering every stage of scholarly communication, from literature search and drafting to peer review, editing and indexing. This raises questions about authorship, credit, quality and the economics of academic publishing.

  • How does AI alter what counts as an original contribution, and who counts as an author?
  • What happens to peer review when reviewers, authors and editors all use AI — and when submission volumes rise sharply?
  • How are commercial publishers using AI and the content they hold, including licensing it for model training?
  • Will AI reinforce dominant paradigms, languages and centres of knowledge production, or widen access for scholars in the Global South and in heterodox traditions?
  • What editorial policies, governance models and alternatives (diamond open access, scholar-led journals) are adequate to this moment?

3. AI, education and the future of universities
AI raises basic questions about the purpose, organisation and funding of higher education. It may reshape institutional strategy, business models and the relationship between universities, states and technology firms.

  • How are universities governing AI adoption, and whose interests shape procurement and partnerships with technology firms?
  • Does AI strengthen the case for mass, low-cost online provision, and with whatconsequences for public universities?
  • How will AI affect the value of degrees, graduate labour markets and the university's credentialing role?
  • What does AI mean for inequality between institutions, countries and groups of students?
  • What visions of the public university can be defended in an age of AI?

4. AI and the transformation of pedagogy and curriculum
AI tools are changing how students learn and how teachers teach. They challenge assumptions about which knowledge and skills a curriculum should prioritise.

  • What should students learn when AI can write, code, summarise and calculate?
  • How does AI change the teacher–student relationship, feedback and the role of tutoring?
  • What are the risks of deskilling, homogenised thinking or over-reliance, and how can teaching counter them?
  • How should disciplines — including economics and the social sciences — integrate critical AI literacy into their curricula?
  • What evidence do we have on learning outcomes, and what does it fail to capture?

5. AI and the redefinition of assessment and academic integrity
AI unsettles the essay, the take-home exam and other established forms of assessment. It also strains existing frameworks of plagiarism and misconduct.

  • What forms of assessment remain meaningful when AI can produce competent written work?
  • How reliable and fair are AI-detection tools, and who bears the cost of their errors?
  • How should academic integrity be redefined: as rule enforcement, as trust, or as a shared scholarly ethic?
  • How do assessment reforms interact with workload, class sizes and institutional pressure on pass rates?
  • What can be learned from institutions and countries that have already redesignedassessment?

Approaches welcomed
Challenge publishes short (up to 4000 words), non-technical and policy-oriented papers. In this context, we welcome theoretical, historical and policy-oriented contributions from economics, political economy, sociology, education studies, labour studies, science and technology studies, and related fields. Papers may draw on quantitative or qualitative methods, case studies of institutions or national systems, and comparative work.

We particularly encourage:

  • contributions that place AI within broader changes in the political economy of higher education, rather than treating it as an isolated technology;
  • evidence from the Global South and from under-studied institutional settings;
  • work that connects the experiences of staff, students and editors with the strategies of institutions, states and firms;
  • interdisciplinary and pluralist perspectives, including heterodox traditions in economics.

We will only be publishing up to a maximum of 10 articles.

Submission and timeline
Authors should first send an extended abstract of up to 250 words, with a short biographical note, to the guest editors. Contributions will be editorially-reviewed. Acceptance of an abstract does not guarantee publication.

item.title: [Call for Papers] Workshop: "From the Origin to the Future of Money" (Austria, March 2027)
item.description:
31.03. - 02.04. 2027 | Linz, Austria

Institute of Philosophy and Scientific Method (JKU Linz, Austria)

Political and scientific debates about the future of money are often underpinned by diverging accounts of money’s origin. This pattern appears to be relatively stable in the history of monetary theory. Carl Menger put forward an explanation of the spontaneous emergence of money as a market phenomenon which is invoked by later members of the Austrian School in their argumentation against state intervention in the monetary system. Georg Friedrich Knapp described money as a “creature of the legal order”; Alfred Mitchell-Innes understood money as credit. Both inspired post-Keynesians and proponents of MMT to advocate for the active construction and management of monetary systems. Karl Marx based his rejection of monetary reform on his view of money as a necessary feature of capitalism which, if abolished, would spontaneously re-originate.

How to best make sense of the connection between descriptive accounts of the origin of money and normative proposals for the future of money? Do investigations into money’s origin allow insights about its “essential nature” which, in turn, has normative implications? Are positions regarding the origin, nature, and politics of money as well as the proper method of investigation embedded in distinct worldviews? Or is the supposed connection merely a result of naturalist fallacies and strategic attempts at persuasion?

Addressing these interdisciplinary questions requires joint efforts by philosophers, economists, and historians. This workshop aims to facilitate such fruitful interaction and cooperation. Topics for submission include but are not limited to:

  • Development of different schools of monetary theory and their interaction
  • Comparing and evaluating theories of the origin of money
  • “What is money”: essentialism vs. nominalism
  • Descriptive and normative aspects of monetary theory
  • Discretionary vs. rule-based monetary policy
  • Contemporary proposals for the future of money (cryptocurrencies, CBDC, MMT, etc.)
  • Methodological individualism and its discontents
  • Methodological problems of different price indices (CPI, OOHPI, …)
  • Worldviews and adversarial collaboration


Confirmed Speakers: Jan Greitens (Westfälische Hochschule), Francesco Guala (University of Milan), Hansjörg Klausinger (Vienna University of Economics and Business), Lukas Starchl (University of Graz), Lea Steininger (London School of Economics and Vienna Institute for International Studies), Richard Sturn (University of Graz)

Workshop theme: The conception of evidence and the shaping of doing economics

The University “Alexandru Ioan Cuza” in Iași, Romania, will host a workshop on 20–21 November 2026 devoted to the nature and role of evidence in economics and other sciences.

In much of modern economics, both mainstream and beyond, the issue of evidence centres on the increasing sophistication of econometric inference. Underpinning this is a confidence that econometric models are sufficiently robust to provide accurate forecasts of economic trends and to illuminate our understanding of phenomena. The rise of experimental game theory within new behaviouralism further augments this allegedly rich evidential base. Our ability to grasp the complexities of the economy continues to grow.

Yet fragilities persist. The failure of the profession to predict — and to understand — the great financial crisis remains emblematic of these limits, and interrogation and reflection are not always apparent in economic thinking. This workshop aims to furnish researchers within the EC2U Alliance with the means to question standard presumptions about the nature of evidence in economics. Through a combination of invited experts, Q&A sessions and group discussions, participants will be encouraged to reflect on different types of evidence, their role in analysis and argumentation, and, more broadly, on the doing of economics.

item.description:
25 November, 2026 | Online | London, UK

Symposium theme: Capitalism in Transformation

With the rise of AI, venture capital, private credit and the far right, our economies are experiencing a deep transformation. After the Global Financial Crisis, much of the political economy literature anticipated a decline in the power of capital interests in advanced market economies. The combination of severe financial distress, populist countermovements, and renewed regulatory intervention was expected to truncate business power and restore state authority vis-à-vis capital.

However, this decline in power did not materialise. In the two decades since the crisis, business power has not diminished, but it has transformed. Asset-management firms now pool vast amounts of global savings, while venture capital and private credit have contributed to an unprecedented concentration of corporate control in private markets. More recently, the rise of AI has accelerated investment flows into technology sectors, potentially ushering in new forms of capital concentration. At the same time, new state-business alliances appear to be forming. We now know that far-right and nationalist political projects do not consistently resist the expansion of capital power. Instead, they appear to increasingly align with concentrated power in finance and technology.

You are warmly invited to take part in CITYPERC Symposium on Capitalism in Transformation on Wednesday, 25 November 2026. The symposium will explore the rise of venture capital, AI, and private credit, as well as the emerging alliances of actors in these markets with the far right. Speakers include Daniela Gabor, Milan Babic, Mònica Clua-Losada, Kean Birch, Franziska Cooiman, Albena Azmanova, Scott James, Photis Lysandrou and Inga Rademacher.
